events.title: Macklemore says Robert Kraft had him dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour after his comments about the Palestinian territories
events.summary: Macklemore said he's off Ed Sheeran's tour after his "Free Palestine" comments. Kristy Sparow/Getty Images Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran's tour after his "Free Palestine" comments, the singer said. Macklemore said Robert Kraft called Sheeran to say the singer would not be welcome in his stadium. Sheeran's band and other opening acts dropped out of the tour in response to Macklemore's removal. Macklemore says he's been kicked off Ed Sheeran's tour because Robert Kraft , the billionaire owner of the NFL's New England Patriots, took issue with his comments about the Palestinian territories. Macklemore had made the comments onstage while opening for Sheeran at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium earlier this month. The singer Pink then reshared criticism of Macklemore, sparking a torrent of backlash for herself. In a lengthy statement shared on Instagram Monday, Macklemore said Kraft called Sheeran amid the firestorm. "Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium," Macklemore said, referring to Kraft's Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. "Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues." In a statement reported by other outlets, Kraft confirmed the stadium opposed his appearing at Sheeran's upcoming shows. "Gillette Stadium has a longstanding commitment to providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech," the statement said, according to local outlet WHDH. "Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line." Messina Touring Group, the tour promoter, said in a statement to Rolling Stone earlier on Monday that Macklemore would not perform on the remainder of Sheeran's tour after several venues said they wouldn't allow him to appear. In a Tuesday post to Instagram , Sheeran wrote that he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and confirmed that he had talked to Kraft, other venues, promoters, and activists in an effort to find a mutual resolution, but that the venue's and promoters' decision "was final." "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he added. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me." "I have spent this week trying to build bridges, to find a solution and unfortunately, was unable to do so," he said. Sheeran's tour band Beoga and the other opening acts — Finneas, Lukas Graham, and Aaron Rowe — all announced Tuesday they were dropping out of the tour, citing the situation with Macklemore. "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas wrote in a statement. Update, September 15, 2026 — This post has been updated to include Sheeran's Tuesday statement and the news that Sheeran's band and other opening acts had dropped out of the tour. events.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
events.summary: Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle. Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems. "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios. "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough." State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products. Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios first reported Monday. Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table. The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems. Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) have also been championing their comprehensive AI regulation bill, the Frontier Act. Zoom out: It has been years since Congress passed multiple pieces of truly big bipartisan legislation, and decades since bipartisan lawmaking on marquee issues was a regular practice. The most common moments when cross-party cooperation sees a renaissance on Capitol Hill these days: crises. Consider what got passed in the 117th Congress, on the heels of the Jan. 6 attack and the COVID pandemic: $1.2 trillion in infrastructure spending , a $280 billion semiconductor and research bill and the first major gun safety law in decades, all with bipartisan majorities. Yes, but: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled that his chamber will not take any action on the AI front before the House leaves for a six-week recess that doesn't end until after Election Day. Johnson said in a CNN interview Sunday that Congress should "not smother American innovation" with overly burdensome AI regulations. President Trump has gone even further in dismissing the urgency of federal AI regulations, writing in a Truth Social post Monday: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." What to watch: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has sounded a considerably more dire note on the issue. A potential House Democratic majority next year may be the place where AI regulation finally finds its footing on Capitol Hill.

events.title: Historic outback pub hits the market as restoration costs soar
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Historic Kalgoorlie-Boulder hotel hits market again amid heritage challenges The Cornwall Hotel was badly damaged in the 1934 Kalgoorlie race riots. ( Supplied: State Library of WA ) The 128-year-old Cornwall Hotel in Boulder has survived riots and earthquakes and has now been listed for sale. It last traded as a pub in 2010 when it was badly damaged by an earthquake, although it has undergone extensive structural repairs. The hotel's interior needs additional restoration work, but ongoing shortages of skilled tradespeople represent a challenge alongside heritage restrictions. A heritage-listed hotel in Western Australia's Goldfields, infamous for its connection to the murders of two police officers a century ago, has hit the market with an asking price of more than $1 million. It is the second time the Cornwall Hotel in Boulder has been listed for sale in the past decade, suggesting the overheated construction market and onerous heritage obligations may be turning off potential buyers. The two-storey hotel was built in 1898, just five years after the discovery of gold at Kalgoorlie. It takes its name from the 19th-Century Cornish miners who flooded into WA during the gold rush and built the pub from locally quarried stone. The Cornwall Hotel received $992,090 from the WA government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund, but structural repairs did not begin until 2016. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) Real estate agent James Brennan described the nine-bedroom hotel as a unique piece of Goldfields history, but conceded the interior "needs a lot of love". He said a mining company needing workers' accommodation could be a potential buyer, as the city faced ongoing accommodation shortages . "A property like this, it needs the right owner, someone who can bring it back to its former glory," he said. "It really is hard to put a price on that history, and obviously it's a beautiful building … heritage does scare people at times, but there's definitely been a lot of interest." The Cornwall Hotel in Boulder circa 1926. ( Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society ) The Cornwall Hotel's most famous former licensee was Evan Clarke, who turned king's evidence following the brutal murders of detectives Inspector John Walsh and Sergeant Alexander Pitman, who were after gold thieves, in 1926. It was rumoured that following the murders, the bodies were taken to the hotel where they were dismembered before being set alight and thrown down disused mineshafts. Detective Inspector John Walsh (left) and Detective Sergeant Alexander Pitman were on the trail of gold thieves when they were murdered. ( Facebook: WA Police Historical Society ) The family of Jack Osmetti, a well-known local sportsman who ran the pub for around 50 years, bought it in 1927. The hotel was badly damaged by fire during Kalgoorlie's 1934 race riots and again by a magnitude-5 earthquake in 2010, but has been extensively repaired. Negotiations with insurers resulted in the building being propped up and fenced off for four years, until matters were finally settled in 2014. The owners then applied for and received $992,090 from the state government's $5 million Goldfields Earthquake Restoration Fund , but structural repairs did not begin until 2016. In the era when the Cornwall Hotel was built, stonemasons constructed enduring public and commercial buildings by combining cheap, highly skilled manual labour with traditional lime mortars and hand-dressed masonry. Today, retired Kalgoorlie stonemason Ken Ball reckoned his 55-year occupation was a "dying trade" and that the demise of historic buildings was a sign of the times. Ken Ball (left) and Eastern Goldfields Historical Society member Arthur Ward with a photograph of the Cornwall Hotel after the 1934 race riots. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) "I've got a lot of good memories here," he said, standing outside the Cornwall Hotel. "I did a lot of work at the old Boulder cemetery, so I would often stop in for a drink on the way home … obviously not since the earthquake, though. "It's a shame to see beautiful old buildings like this wasting away, and you'd love to see them get a new lease on life, but finding tradesmen is hard enough, let alone heritage-qualified tradesmen." Heritage projects 'astronomically harder' The City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder offers grants of up to $50,000 to private owners of heritage-listed buildings, but uptake has been low in recent years.

events.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards files complaint against House Ethics
events.summary: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules. Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace. Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case. The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier. The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate. Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint. He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response. Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed. The committee declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios. Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous gifts, including jewelry worth over $1,000, as well as "designer purses, guns , shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics panel found. What they're saying: "He has no remorse, and now he's trying to turn the tables and say somehow ethics did something wrong," Rep. Teresa Leger- Fernandez (D-NM), the chair of the Democratic Women's Caucus, told Axios. "It just shows you how hard to touch the man is," she added of Edwards. DeSaulnier told Axios he had not yet read Edwards' complaint but was confident the committee followed the proper process.

events.title: Fishers fund review in last-ditch effort to overturn gillnet ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Great Barrier Reef gillnet fishers say consultant's report shows they can be sustainable Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Nathan Rynn is one of 25 fishers in Queensland using gillnets to catch fish by their fins and gills. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) East coast inshore fishery operators say a report by consultants FishListic shows positive signs that they can meet international Marine Stewardship Council standards after consultation. The Queensland Seafood Industry Association has sent findings to governments in the hope of overturning a June 2027 ban on gillnets within the Great Barrier Reef Heritage Area. The office of Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett says it will undertake a robust review when it receives the full report. Commercial fishers in north Queensland are hoping a new report will convince the state and federal governments to reverse a planned ban on gillnets within the Great Barrier Reef. Operators in the fishing zone have commissioned a report they say shows their netting practices are likely to pass international sustainability standards. Temporary licences were introduced in 2024 to allow commercial fishers to continue using gillnets ahead of the planned phase-out in 2027. The Queensland Seafood Industry Association, working with the operators, would not release the full report to the ABC, saying it was "commercial in confidence". It did, however, release a summary of findings, which the ABC verified as being accurate by the report's authors, sustainable seafood consultants FishListic. Townsville commercial fisher Nathan Rynn says results from the report are promising. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) Fisher Nathan Rynn said the association hoped to use the report to obtain a Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) "blue tick" on their boats and products to show the fishery was sustainable. "I'm sort of positive about the net fishery moving forward, albeit the legislation issues," Mr Rynn said. "I think we can overcome that and have the best-managed fishery on the planet … but we'll actually have the accreditation behind it, possibly." According to the released section of the report, FishListic said it found the fishery would meet half of the MSC's standards without any conditions imposed and could pass others after further consultation. The company reviewed the ecological risk of four threatened species that had interactions with the large mesh nets. Great hammerhead sharks, scalloped hammerhead sharks, green sawfish and hawksbill turtles all returned a medium risk of being impacted by the nets, down from high risk under the current Queensland government assessment. Scalloped hammerhead sharks are one of two species with recorded fatal interactions with gillnets since 2024. ( Scalloped Hammerhead Shark Sphyrna Lewini , Kris Mikael Krister , CC BY 3.0 ) Several dolphin, marine turtle, and shark species listed as high risk under the 2021 study were not analysed in the FishListic report. The company did not conduct site inspections but used public data, along with camera footage and data logs provided by fishers, to assess the MSC criteria. The Queensland Seafood Industry Association's David Bobberman said the east coast inshore fishery produced between 200 and 300 tonnes of seafood annually. Mr Bobberman said consultation and further research projects would likely be required before the fishery could receive a blue tick and "certified sustainable seafood" labelling. "To be clear, it's not MSC-certified at the moment, but it's been pre-assessed, and the pre-assessor has given them a pass mark," he said. Gillnets are anchored to the ocean floor and held vertically in the water. ( Flickr : Virginia Sea Grant ) The MSC uses third-party auditors to conduct in-person reviews of fishing practices against international standards, following a pre-assessment. Criteria include the sustainability of fish stocks, protection of marine species and habitat, and management strategy. Mr Bobberman said the fishery impact had been greatly reduced since 2024 with fewer operators, and gillnetters now trained under a sustainable fishing program. "We've gone from over 200 available licences to gillnet within the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park to 25," he said. Mr Bobberman said he did not consider any alternative gear as viable replacements, with line fishing too limited, and tunnel nets "too selective" in when and where they could be used. Wild barramundi and king threadfin salmon are target species for gillnet operators.

events.title: Iran war has cost on average $246 million per day in its first five months, CBO finds
events.summary: The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates the Iran war has cost the Pentagon $38.1 billion through Aug. 1 and could cost another $2 billion to $3 billion for each additional month of fighting. The U.S. has used as much as two-thirds of its missile-defense interceptors since June 2025; replenishing them could take at least five years. The war is projected to keep weighing on inflation, adding 0.5 percentage points to inflation metrics by early 2027 as energy costs spread through the economy, the CBO said. The U.S. war with Iran cost the Pentagon an estimated $38.1 billion through Aug. 1 and could cost another $2 billion to $3 billion for each additional month of fighting, according to a report released Tuesday by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. More than half of the cost has come from replacing missiles and other munitions used during the conflict. Increased flying hours cost another $10.4 billion, while higher fuel prices added $2.7 billion, CBO estimated. The war has led fuel prices around the world to rise since President Donald Trump launched it Feb. 28. The war has also consumed as much as two-thirds of the nation's missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, largely as a result of the U.S. helping defend Israel against Iranian attacks, leaving the U.S. with reduced inventories for several years, CBO warned. "Rebuilding DoD's inventory of interceptors would probably take at least five years — even if production was increased," CBO said in the report, which Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., requested. He is the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee. The CBO estimates follow the first comprehensive accounting of the war's cost and military toll , released late Monday by the Defense Department's inspector general. The two accountings came to similar conclusions. The release of the new calculations could fuel debate over whether the cost of the war, which Trump initially said would last only weeks, is worth it. Democrats are campaigning against the war ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. election and pointing to higher costs for fuel, food and other things linked with the conflict, which Trump has framed as preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons. Trump says Kennedy Center will stay closed unless his name is added back Iran war has cost on average $246 million per day in its first five months: CBO Republican Rep. Massie seeks Hegseth’s impeachment over Iran Trump calls Supreme Court mail ballot ruling ‘big loss for Republicans’ The shortage of missiles could become "especially problematic" in a conflict with an adversary possessing large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles, CBO said, specifically citing China and a potential conflict over Taiwan. The war has also raised consumer prices by reducing oil and natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and disrupting Red Sea shipping. CBO estimated that by the first quarter of 2027, the war will have raised year-over-year inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index — which is the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure — by 0.5 percentage points. Core PCE inflation is expected to be 0.3 points higher as energy costs ripple through supply chains, CBO said. "The price of almost every product reflects shipping costs," CBO said. By early 2027, gasoline and other fuels will account for about 40% of the war's effect on consumer prices, CBO said. U.S. crude topped $106 Tuesday and Brent rose above $109 after Saudi Arabia reportedly canceled shipments following the closure of a major pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, regular gasoline averaged about $4.33 per gallon nationally, up almost 18 cents from a week earlier and $1.15 from a year ago, according to AAA . CBO and Pentagon calculate war's costs The Pentagon estimated that the war had cost $33.4 billion as of June 29: $7.4 billion in incremental operating costs, $22.3 billion to replace expended munitions and $3.7 billion in equipment losses. The pace of weapons use created " strategic inventory shortfalls ," the Defense Department watchdog said. Shortages of solid rocket motors, explosives, propellants and skilled workers have complicated efforts to replenish U.S. stockpiles. Iranian strikes also damaged or destroyed "hundreds of buildings and structures" at bases across eight Middle Eastern countries, according to Monday's DOD IG report. Dozens of aircraft have been damaged or destroyed, including four F-15E fighter jets, an F-35A, seven KC-135 refueling aircraft, seven helicopters and more than 30 drones. The F-35A costs as much as $92 million per plane , while the F-15E, which is no longer produced, cost $31.1 million in 1998, according to the U.S. Air Force. The Pentagon report noted State Department costs of $79.2 million for evacuations and other contingencies for people from the region when the war began.

events.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
events.summary: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach the 218 required to discharge the bill, though Democratic leadership is encouraging members to sign on. Massie said he views that as just a logistical problem: "I haven't found any Democrat who's against it." Behind the scenes: Massie and Mace are focusing their recruitment efforts on Republicans who may have less to lose from crossing Trump. "I've got one hero slot left," Massie told Axios. Massie said he's talking to members in districts "where they're polling 10 points down," arguing they can either stay off the petition and risk losing anyway or sign it and make the issue part of their reelection pitch. Mace told Axios she is also "talking to Republicans who are leaving, and some Republican districts that we need to focus in on now." The intrigue: Boebert could provide the fourth Republican signature, but Massie says he doesn't expect the Republicans who took the political risk last year to do it again. "Anybody who did the first one is not obligated to put their head in the guillotine again," Massie said when asked about Boebert. "I think it's somebody else's turn." "Ralph Norman did it. He's a new one, and I think there are other new ones out there that we can get," he added. Between the lines: Massie is again accusing Johnson of manipulating the House calendar to deny him the time needed to force a vote. Johnson recently canceled two of the House's three remaining September workweeks. "He got a call from somebody that's above his pay grade that said, 'Take those two days off the calendar. Don't you dare give Massie the runway to get that plane off the ground,'" Massie said. Johnson, after calling Massie "stupid" for suggesting the House would add recess time, then formally moved to cancel session weeks, as Massie had predicted.

events.title: Target offers worker dress-code options harkening back to 'Tar-zhay.
events.summary: The name of Target's employee apparel Collection 186 is a reference to the trademark red shade Pantone 186. Target Target employees are getting a new line of approved apparel options for work. The collection, designed by style icon Isaac Mizrahi, features the company's trademark shade of red. "It's also to create that feeling of a little bit of swagger," Target's chief stores officer told BI. Target workers are getting a stylish new way to follow the retailer's dress code. The company said Tuesday it is offering employees access to a line of apparel in the bullseye's trademark red, designed by style icon Isaac Mizrahi. Target implemented tighter dress code requirements earlier this summer for store workers as part of new CEO Michael Fiddelke's larger effort to elevate the shopping experience and return the company to growth . The new rules require blue or beige pants, and that tops be primarily Target-shaded red. Social media reaction to the policy change was mixed. "Dress code is important because we want our team members to be recognizable to our guests," chief stores officer Adrienne Costanzo told Business Insider in an interview ahead of the announcement. "A level of professionalism and how we show up for our guests matters." Only active Target employees can buy the new Collection 186. Target The new apparel harkens back to Target's "cheap chic" aesthetic — pioneered by Mizrahi — that earned the brand the "Tar-zhay" moniker. " Store team members are the heart and soul of Target, and I was thrilled to contribute to their experience in the way I know best," Mizrahi said in a statement to Business Insider. Starting at $10 before employee discounts, the 16-piece collection joins Target's employee-exclusive workwear line dubbed Collection 186, which refers to the trademark red shade Pantone 186. The limited-edition items are slated to be available on October 5, and some items will not be replenished if they sell out. Target said the collection includes performance fabric shirts, as well as layers such as track jackets, cardigans, blazers, and vests. Stores already provide basic vests that employees may borrow if they're not wearing an allowed shade of red. The company said says all items in the 186 assortment are optional for employees, and that dress code compliant clothing may be purchased anywhere. Costanzo said the collection has something for those who are more focused on performance as well as more fashion-minded employees. The new collection is a mix of functional and fashionable items. Target "It's also to create that feeling of a little bit of swagger. Like, this collection's for us, the Target team," she said. "And oh, by the way, someone as great as Isaac has helped influence it." Costanzo credited Mizrahi for inspiring her to join Target more than 20 years ago. "Part of the reason that I thought Target was cool enough to come and work after a fashion design degree is because of Isaac Mizrahi," she said. Mizrahi returned to Target this summer as creative director at large, a role in which he advises on product design and aims to strengthen the company's cultural relevance. Part of his philosophy is the principle that good design should be accessible to all. "If we're going to be asking our team to elevate the experience, we need to be supporting them to do that," Costanzo said. "I'm really excited about it. I have my eye on a couple pieces." events.title: ‘Now We Can Know Everything and Do Anything,’ Jensen Huang Says at Dreamforce
events.summary: That was the message NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang brought to Salesforce Dreamforce Tuesday, joining CEO Marc Benioff onstage in an appearance that coincided with the announcement of Koa — Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super. Huang didn’t just take the stage. He walked into the crowd — threading through the audience at Moscone Center, mic in hand, with Benioff alongside. “We’re all following you, bro,” Benioff told Huang at one point, drawing applause. “With electricity, we could power everything,” Huang said, tracing the arc of industrial revolutions. “With the internet, you can find anything. And now, with artificial intelligence as an infrastructure layer across the planet, we can know everything and do anything.” That arc led directly to the announcement. Salesforce’s first reasoning model was built by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset drawn from nearly three decades of enterprise CRM deployments. When Benioff asked Huang about AI safety, Huang was direct. “Safety is paramount in a lot of ways. It’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem. We’re developing computing systems after all … If you build a product or a service and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability or safety, then don’t release it.” He reiterated that innovation and leadership should coincide with safety and security . “Innovation, speed and safe products — it’s a false choice,” Huang said. “You could definitely have both at the same time. So run as fast as you can. But if you feel at any given point in time the company’s out of control, or the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right.” Throughout his talk, Huang offered a positive vision for the future of AI. He noted he was among the first to push back on the notion that AI would end the software industry. He also pushed back on the idea that AI is a threat to jobs. “As a result of our ambition, and with the productivity boost we get from AI, the sky’s the limit,” he added. “Engage AI. Don’t get left behind.” “Every company, every enterprise, every country would become an AI company,” Huang said. “It’s going to be an agentic enterprise.” “The sky is especially the limit for our Trailblazers,” Benioff said, referring to the company’s customer and developer community. “I think this technology, the way it empowers people … the technology can partner with them to do this in incredible new ways.” Because NVIDIA Nemotron is open, Salesforce was able to fine-tune and run the model entirely within its own infrastructure. Salesforce controls the weights, the model runs on Salesforce’s systems and no customer data is used during training or inference. “Not a single byte of customer data was used,” said Rohan Kumar, Salesforce’s president of platform and engineering, who introduced Koa before Huang took the stage. Open models went from 30% at the beginning of last year to now some 70%, Huang explained. “People are both adopting closed models at exponential rates, but also building their own custom AIs — because every single software company is an AI company, and every single enterprise is going to be an agentic and AI enterprise.” NVIDIA is one of them — running on Salesforce across sales, service, marketing and operations, and currently piloting Agentforce for customer-support workflows. Koa was built using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with NVIDIA NeMo RL, NeMo Gym and NeMo AutoModel. The training corpus covers synthetic enterprise scenarios across 14+ industries — manufacturing, financial services, healthcare and travel. In Salesforce’s CRM Bench, a model benchmark that includes a suite of real-world tasks like updating an opportunity, routing a case, or scheduling a follow-up, Koa already matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions with 3x fewer errors. Koa is already running inside Salesforce, powering an employee agent in Slack, and is moving into customer pilots in October as a customer-selectable model in Agentforce, starting with Formula 1, UChicago Medicine, Baxter Credit Union, 1-800Accountant, Engine and Xero. General availability is expected winter 2026 in U.S. regions. events.title: Satya Nadella says there’s one ‘common sense’ rule AI companies need to follow
events.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he has one simple AI rule to follow, which is to keep humans in control. Sven Hoppe/picture alliance via Getty Images Satya Nadella said powerful AI should serve humanity and remain under human control. Teach leaders are weighing in on AI safety amid calls for slower development. Nadella said he welcomes third-party testing and that major bugs should halt development. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has a straightforward rule for companies building powerful AI: Keep people in charge. "We should do what it takes to build stuff that serves humanity first and is in human control," Nadella told the audience at the All-In Summit on Tuesday. "You've got to have choice. You have to have competition. You have to have all kinds of business models, whether they're open weights, closed weights, what have you." "You know, it's kind of crazy that we have to start with that level of common sense, but I think it's a good place," Nadella added. "I want my privacy. I want to be able to embed my knowledge in a set of weights I control. My IP shouldn't leak." Nadella's comments come amid an intensifying debate over whether frontier AI companies should slow development to address emerging risks. Last week, an Anthropic researcher quit and said that leading AI companies are "gambling with our lives." The debate has also been fueled by an incident in which an OpenAI model escaped a research sandbox and accessed Hugging Face 's production infrastructure. The model had not yet undergone alignment training and was operating with reduced safeguards. Prominent AI leaders have since then weighed in. While OpenAI and Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, called for slower AI development in favor of more guardrails, other tech leaders like Jensen Huang , the Nvidia CEO, have said that an AI slowdown won't happen. Nadella said companies should take as much time as necessary to test advanced models, including welcoming third-party testers and taking a page from the engineer playbook. "It's possible that they see stuff which are showstoppers before the rest, and if you see a showstopper, stop the show to fix the bugs," Nadella said of the AI industry. "One of the biggest things you learn as an early engineering lead is how to deal with a showstopper bug. Do you stop and fix, or you defer, or you go in and say, 'Hey, this is such an edge case?'" "In fact, I love this idea of having third-party testers," Nadella added. "We should take all the time we want to test things." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
events.summary: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared on Instagram Tuesday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour came not from him, but from the promoters. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." Sheeran also wrote on Instagram that he didn't want his Loop Tour drawn into a public discussion around the war in Gaza. "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," Sheeran wrote on IG. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated." He added: "I have my personal views on the devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way." Zoom out: The turmoil over Sheeran's concert tour raises broader questions about political speech at concerts. As Rolling Stone notes, several stadiums that opposed Macklemore's appearance are publicly owned. One such venue is Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which faced calls to cancel Ye's shows earlier this year due to his past antisemitic comments. The bottom line: Sheeran has tried to keep politics off his stage. The fight over Gaza has now made that neutrality difficult to maintain.

events.title: Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, at an event at the White House in June. Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee launched an investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s relationship with a Russian oligarch who paid for much of Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., sent two letters on Monday to the White House and Trump Jr. requesting records related to Trump Jr.’s financial relationship with the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. “The secretive, close relationship between the son of a sitting U.S. President and a member of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious national security and public corruption concerns,” Garcia wrote. Garcia told Trump Jr. it “may be the most serious allegation against you to date.” The letter to Trump Jr. asked for documents including Trump Jr.’s communications with Kremlev and “financial records of all purchases made for your wedding by foreign nationals.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” Trump Jr. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Garcia’s investigation. The letters were prompted by a ProPublica investigation published Monday , which revealed that Kremlev secretly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars of expenses for Trump Jr.’s wedding. That included renting out a private island in the Bahamas for multiple nights. The wedding guest list numbered around 50, including Jared Kushner and other members of the Trump family. Kremlev, who first met Trump Jr. recently, also attended the intimate affair with a large group of other Russians. Kremlev is close to Putin and serves as the head of the International Boxing Association, a scandal-plagued sports group that has been financed by the Russian state-owned energy giant Gazprom. The wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions. Kremlev’s press office previously told ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. “have a friendly relationship” and that they don’t talk politics. After ProPublica’s story was published, Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, released a joint statement confirming Kremlev’s role. “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us,” they said in a statement published on her Instagram account. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.” They added, “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.” The couple also drew a distinction between the ceremony itself, which was just family, and the rest of the wedding weekend. In a statement released by the White House after the story was published, President Donald Trump echoed that. “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding,” he said. “It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal!” The couple exchanged vows on Friday, May 22, on a private island in the Bahamas. The wedding festivities then continued for two days. The Saturday, May 23, event, which Kremlev paid for, was held on the same island as the ceremony. (“Night 2. One Love!” Bettina Trump posted about the Saturday festivities on Instagram.) The Sunday reception was held a roughly 10-minute boat ride away on a neighboring private island, rented out by Kremlev. At the Sunday reception, the couple had their first dance, with Bettina Trump wearing her wedding dress, and ate a five-tier wedding cake topped with a miniature bride and groom.  Afterward, the couple’s wedding planner talked to Hello! magazine about planning the three-day affair with Bettina Trump. “She wanted a progression,” said the planner, Lewis Miller. “The ceremony was very serene and pretty and soft, and the dinner was very elegant, and then the next night was much more colorful, and then the last night was more kind of cool and fun tropical vibes.” Read More Donald Trump Jr.’s Bahamas Wedding Was Secretly Bankrolled by Russian Oligarch Close to Putin The post Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: The AI data center boom is colliding with cities scarred by big industry
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Across the country, Americans are debating how their lives might change if new AI data centers are built in their backyards. Data center companies and their customers are promising new jobs and economic growth, but that pitch hasn’t won over a majority of Americans who oppose data center construction in their area, often over environmental and energy concerns. For activist Shawmar Pitts, these concerns aren’t theoretical. He knows better than anyone what it’s like to live in the shadow of American industrialization. A lifelong resident of the Grays Ferry neighborhood in Southwest Philadelphia, Pitts grew up next to what was then the East Coast’s largest oil refinery , which shut down after an explosion in 2019. Though many of his friends and family suffered from chronic health conditions, he didn’t realize what might have caused these illnesses until he encountered the environmental justice group Philly Thrive , which was tabling in his neighborhood in 2018 about a proposed oil refinery expansion. “I read the information they had on the table about how living near the refinery affects you, and I’m looking at all the sicknesses on this paper, and I’m like, ‘My mother has this, my sister has that, my next-door neighbor suffers from this’ — every house, someone has something on that list,” Pitts told TechCrunch. “From that point, I was all the way in.” Pitts, who is now the managing co-director of that same organization, is among those leading the charge for a data center moratorium in Philadelphia. While there have been no formal proposals for construction yet, city officials have identified two potential sites : one in Northeast Philadelphia and the other in Pitts’ Grays Ferry neighborhood. Data center opposition from local residents isn’t unique to Philadelphia. Residents across the United States have pushed back against new data center construction, particularly those living in cities and towns with finite resources. But the pushback has been particularly swift from people living in communities where big industry’s mark is still felt. “We don’t want data centers,” Philly Thrive board president Sonya Sanders said at a rally on Monday at Philadelphia’s City Hall. “We don’t want the pollution, we don’t want the noise, and we know they’re not going to bring us more jobs.” Sanders’ husband, who was also a resident of Grays Ferry, died of a rare bone cancer in 2020. She said he didn’t smoke or drink, and she believes that emissions from the refinery caused his illness. “In my eyes, they killed him,” she said at the rally. “The pollution killed him. I believe he would be here today if he wasn’t silently murdered, because it was the pursuit of profit that killed him.” A Philadelphia data center may not have as severe an environmental impact as the now-defunct Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery, which processed up to 335,000 barrels of crude oil daily. But the international race to dominate the AI industry has become so extreme that by 2035, BloombergNEF predicts that U.S. data centers will consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined. That’s almost double the firm’s projection from nine months ago. Natural gas burns a lot cleaner than other fossil fuels, like oil, but it’s far from harmless. Burning one cubic foot of natural gas releases the equivalent of 60 grams of carbon dioxide , and additional data center demand is expected to generate an extra 1 million metric tons of greenhouse gas pollution each day, which is about 12% of all present day U.S. greenhouse gas emissions . Harvard University researchers found in 2021 that fossil fuel air pollution is responsible for one in five deaths worldwide , a staggering figure that is bound to increase in the age of AI. “A typical data center planned in Pennsylvania has hundreds of diesel engines that spew air pollution, and even if they’re supposedly reserved for emergencies , the government has already said that the data center should use those rather than drawing from an overstressed electrical grid during some heat waves,” said Clean Air Council attorney Annie Fox at the rally. “We can expect that to get more frequent… Fossil fuel-hungry data centers will worsen climate change, making those heatwaves more frequent and severe.” Concerned citizens across the country do seem to be getting through to their officials. In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order that temporarily prevents the state from approving new permits for large projects. “Progress shouldn’t arrive with a higher utility bill, deleted water supply, or noise pollution,” Hochul said at a press conference. “These data centers can only be built, should only be built in places that want them.” Data center moratoriums have also been approved in a number of U.S.

events.title: Trump says Kennedy Center will stay closed without renovation unless his name is added back
events.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts from returning President Donald Trump's name to the center in some fashion, months after the same judge ordered Trump's name removed from its facade. The Kennedy Center's board, which is largely appointed by Trump, again voted to close the center for renovations, amid what the board says are pressing financial concerns. The center will be closed to visitors indefinitely. Trump said that the center will close immediately, and that renovations will not begin unless and until a higher court reverses the decision to remove his name from the facility's official name. A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the Kennedy Center board's effort to return President Donald Trump 's name to the center in some form, months after the same judge ordered his name removed from the facade of the Washington, D.C., performing arts facility. Later Tuesday, the Kennedy Center's board, largely appointed by Trump, again voted to close the facility for renovations, amid what the board says are pressing financial concerns. The board previously voted in March to shutter for renovations. Judge Christopher Cooper in May blocked that decision while leaving the door open for the facility to be closed for emergency or necessary renovations. It is not clear whether Cooper will agree that the board's latest vote suffices to meet those conditions. Trump, in a statement, said: "The closing will take place immediately." But the president added that the renovations and reconstruction of the center will not begin unless and until a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court rules Trump's name can be restored to the center's official name. Democracy Defenders Action, an advocacy group that is providing legal services to Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the center's board, said the Kennedy Center is barred from closing until Cooper lifts a preliminary injunction he issued in May in federal district court in D.C. Beatty's lawyers said that Trump during Tuesday's board meeting "verbally berated" Beatty "for her efforts to save the center." In response, they said, "She strongly condemned his efforts to destroy the treasured American institution." Beatty, in a statement, said, "For years, the Kennedy Center has planned to undergo phased renovations, in which we both renovate and maintain some performances." "This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate. But donors, patrons, and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump," Beatty said. "Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity," she said. "That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee." Beatty's lawyers, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, in a statement said, "The Board's latest shutdown vote is more of the same failure and abuse that has characterized this administration's treatment of the Kennedy Center." "The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away," the lawyers said. "Now the Board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We'll see the Defendants in court." In his new court order Tuesday, Cooper said he agreed that inscribing Trump's name on the building to honor his role in renovating the center or renaming the grounds violated the terms of the permanent injunction he issued in May directing the president's name be removed from the facility's official name. "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Cooper wrote in his order shortly after overseeing a conference in court on the issue. "The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted," Cooper wrote. Hours later, the Department of Justice appealed Cooper's ruling to the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The center's board, in an Aug. 13 resolution, said it intended "to recognize and honor President Trump's future existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the Center." The board said it would inscribe Trump's name on the center's building so that it would read, "The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," with the words "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump" underneath. The board also said it would name the center's physical grounds "The President Donald J. Trump Plaza." It might make 2027 a breeze 36 minutes ago Apple iPhone Duo makes developers think in folds 1 day ago Watch out: Apple timepiece can grab snippets of conversation without both speakers' consent 5 days ago Apple hawks $2k folding fondleslab 6 days ago Asahi Linux takes on Apple M3, minus a few creature comforts 8 days ago Apple has addressed more than 260 CVEs across all of its operating systems, browsers, and other software products, marking the largest single patch cycle in Cupertino's history. While this CVE count is hardly notable compared to some vendors - hello, Microsoft’s record-breaking 974 bugs disclosed earlier this month - it does set a company record for Apple. It also reflects the new reality of AI-driven bug hunting , as models become exponentially better and faster at finding security vulnerabilities. However, the flip side of the AI coin we were promised - that models would also excel at writing patches and automatically fixing software and systems - yeah, that hasn't happened yet. The silver lining for everyone updating their Apple products right now (including this humble vulture): none of the vulnerabilities are listed as being under active exploitation. Of course, that may change very quickly as attackers are, at this very moment, looking to exploit the newly disclosed bugs, too. And we promise you that they are using AI. Apple’s latest mobile and operating system versions, iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, released on Monday, also address a record 122 and 204 security vulnerabilities, respectively, across phone, iPad, and computer operating systems. Of these hundreds of CVEs, however, there are only ten (by our count) that AI is directly credited with finding. Just two of the iPhone and iPad CVEs fixed with iOS 27 credit a coding agent or AI assistant with finding them. These include CVE-2026-65410, a vuln that exists in iPhone and iPad AVE video encoders, that can cause unexpected system termination. Apple credited AI-bug-finding firm Calif, along with Claude and Anthropic Research, with finding and reporting this security flaw. Then there's CVE-2026-65409, a type-confusion issue in iOS’ Foundation framework that can be abused to cause a denial of service, also found by Calif - specifically human researcher Bruce Dang - in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research. Some of the more interesting and serious iOS bugs fixed with the newest update aren’t listed as found by AI. These include CVE-2026-43689, a privilege-escalation flaw that could allow an app to gain root access. Apple credited Nosebeard Labs’ Andreas Jaegersberger and Ro Achterberg with reporting this bug. Additionally, CVE-2026-65406, a logic-issue flaw due to improper validation in Background Assets, could be abused to access sensitive user data. Background Assets is an Apple framework that lets you download large files and content in the background before a user opens the app for the first time. Baidu Security researcher Ye Zhang spotted this one. Meanwhile, the new macOS 27 update that addresses 204 vulns also fixes both the AI hunted bugs: CVE-2026-65410 and CVE-2026-65409. Plus, it credits AI helpers with discovering eight others, including one especially nasty flaw that could lead to remote code execution through the CUPS printer interface. Let’s start with that one. CVE-2026-43692 is a validation issue in CUPS that can be exploited by a remote user to either terminate the app or execute malicious code. Aaron Grattafiori and the Nvidia AI Red Team receive credit for disclosing this flaw. CVE-2026-64790 in CUPS can be exploited to gain elevated privileges. Grattafiori and the Nvidia AI Red Team again get credit for the win. CVE-2026-43791, a validation issue in StorageKit, can be abused to read files. Grattafiori, the Nvidia AI Red Team, Meridian Miftari, and Amy from amys.website disclosed this flaw to Apple. CVE-2026-43690 is a race-condition bug in the Server Message Block (SMB) network communication protocol.

events.title: AI researcher whose apocalypse warning went viral outlines his disagreements with Anthropic leadership
events.summary: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon shed more light on why he left the AI giant. Bloomberg/Getty Images Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon held an AMA on X. Coxon explained more about why he decided to leave Anthropic. He also poked fun at his short time at the AI giant. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon detailed his disagreements with the AI giant during a Tuesday AMA on X. "If the race is inevitable you should not contribute," Coxon wrote. Coxon said that Anthropic leadership is wrong to follow a "consequentialist philosophy" about why it needs to participate in pushing the frontier of AI research. Specifically, Coxon called out Anthropic's push for RSI, or recursive self-improvement, the process by which AI models could improve themselves and build their own successors. "They largely initiated the recent race to RSI, because of a belief in its inevitability," Coxon wrote. "Note that OpenAI had to shed a bunch of dead weight like Sora because Anthropic was going for the jugular." 0. The core disagreement was about the inevitability of a race 1. I think leadership is way too paranoid about China and the US government. They don’t believe it will be possible to negotiate. 2. They largely initiated the recent race to RSI, because of a belief in its… — Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 15, 2026 Coxon's profile exploded last week after he published an explanation for his resignation from Anthropic, which he joined following his time at OpenAI. Coxon said that neither lab was following the best course. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon wrote in his resignation announcement. Coxon also warned that internally, AI workers are concerned about whether the technology they are building will turn on humanity. "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," Coxon wrote. "This is not a marketing stunt." On Tuesday, Coxon also said that Anthropic's leadership is "way too paranoid about China and the US government." "They don't believe it will be possible to negotiate," he wrote. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has repeatedly expressed uneasiness about how other AI companies might approach safety if Anthropic is the only frontier lab to slow down. "If we go too slow, I still believe that the wrong people will be in charge of the technology," Amodei recently told CNN's Anderson Cooper. "And that, again, will bring the probability of things going wrong very high." In addition to other companies, Amodei has expressed concerns about what would happen if authoritarian governments win the AI race. For his part, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently told Time Magazine that the company "fell behind where we wanted to be." As part of a refocus on its core mission, OpenAI sunsetted projects like Sora, its TikTok-esque video app. In recent days, AI leaders have tried to band together to discuss ways to slow the pace of development. Over the weekend, Amodei published a call for frontier companies like Anthropic "to pace" their advancements and to use the time to focus on AI safety issues like alignment, the work to make sure AI models comply with their instructions. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain." Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis all expressed agreement with Amodei's broader point. Other parts of the AMA were more lighthearted. One user asked about Coxon's relatively short time at Anthropic, a point his critics have tried to use to undermine his claims. "Which month was your favorite at Anthropic? Month 1 or month 2?" the user asked. Coxon replied, "Month 2 (of 4)." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Americans' incomes rose and poverty fell in 2025, Census Bureau says
events.summary: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, new Census Bureau data shows, as the official poverty rate declined to 10.2%. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent highlighted the report during House testimony. The Fed is meeting this week to decide whether inflation still warrants higher interest rates. Americans' inflation-adjusted incomes rose and poverty declined in 2025, according to new Census Bureau data released Tuesday, as the Federal Reserve meets to decide whether inflation still requires higher interest rates. Real median household income rose by 2.6% to $87,460 last year, the Census Bureau reported as part of a suite of data releases Tuesday. The poverty rate fell by a nearly half-point to 10.2%. The poverty threshold for a family of four last year was $32,970. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent celebrated the data, which were released as he was testifying to a House committee about the economy. The Census Bureau data are "several inconvenient facts" for the Trump administration's political opponents, he said. Trump says Kennedy Center will stay closed unless his name is added back Iran war has cost on average $246 million per day in its first five months: CBO Republican Rep. Massie seeks Hegseth’s impeachment over Iran Trump calls Supreme Court mail ballot ruling ‘big loss for Republicans’ Democrats used the committee hearing to assail Bessent over high gas prices and other economic strains. The average rate for new 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose above 7% last week. Prices increases by 3.4% in August from the year before, as measured by consumer price index. The Census data covers 2025 and doesn't account for recent changes in inflation or other economic shifts since the Iran war started. But for the first year of Trump's presidency, the data show the median American household's income rose even after adjusting for inflation . The agency doesn't break down the causes for the improvements' in Americans' livelihoods. The underlying data suggest that an improving labor market helped boost household income. The decline in poverty appeared to be concentrated among families with children and working-age families, rather than among retirees. Another measure of poverty that accounts for families' gains from the social safety net was unchanged for 2025. That may come under pressure as Republican's tax-and-policy law enacted in the summer of 2025 is phased in. The measure known as the "Big, Beautiful Bill" cut taxes on some working families but paid for it in part by reducing federal outlays through tightening restrictions on parts of programs for low-income people. The Congressional Budget Office projects that spending on food stamps, known as SNAP, will fall by $211 billion through 2035 years as a result of the law because fewer people will be eligible for nutrition assistance. Meanwhile the Fed is on the precipice of raising its benchmark short-term interest rate. New Chairman Kevin Warsh has said he is concerned about inflation. The Fed's tool to fight inflation — interest rates — is a blunt instrument. By raising rates, the Fed raises borrowing costs across the economy. That slows price increases by generally weakening economic growth. The Fed has to weigh that risk against the damage inflation does to Americans' livelihoods. Fed officials have frequently pointed out that price increases weigh most heavily on the lowest tier of earners who have the least ability to change their spending plans. The Fed will announce its rate decision Wednesday afternoon.

events.title: 3M, DuPont and more to face lawsuit on Pfas in US firefighters’ protective gear
events.summary: Connecticut plaintiffs say ‘forever chemicals’ in turnout gear increase risk of cancer by absorption and inhalation A federal judge on Tuesday said more than 20 defendants including 3M , DuPont and Honeywell must ⁠face claims by Connecticut firefighters who said their protective gear was contaminated by toxic “forever chemicals” that increased their risk of cancer. Lawyers ⁠for 13 firefighter union ⁠organizations and ​12 individual firefighters said “turnout gear” that shields against extreme heat and flames leached the chemicals through absorption into skin, ingestion and inhalation. ⁠They have called the proposed class action the first to exclusively target firefighter gear containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or Pfas . US district judge Alvin Thompson ⁠in Hartford, Connecticut , said the unions had “organizational” standing to seek damages, and firefighters could seek damages ​and medical monitoring even if they had ‌no outward symptoms of disease. The judge also said the plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that 3M, one of ‌the largest manufacturers of Pfas , owed a duty to warn about the risks and committed negligence. Pfas in firefighters’ protective gear included 3M’s Scotchlite reflective material and DuPont’s Kevlar, while Honeywell manufactured turnout gear, according to the complaint. Some DuPont liabilities now belong to two spinoffs, Chemours and Corteva. Lawyers for 3M, DuPont, Chemours, Corteva and Honeywell did not immediately ‌respond to requests for comment. Jennifer Sclar, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said the decision was significant because it found that prolonged exposure to ​Pfas from turnout gear justified legal standing. In seeking dismissals, 3M said there were no plausible claims tying Scotchlite to firefighters’ gear, while other defendants said there was no allegation that the gear “failed to serve its function of protecting firefighters from the hazards of fighting fires”. The lawsuit ⁠began in June 2024. Pfas are found in hundreds of consumer and ​commercial products including cosmetics, nonstick ​pans and stain-resistant clothing. They are known ​as “forever chemicals” because they do not break down easily in the human ​body or environment and have been linked to various health issues. In 2023, DuPont, 3M and two other companies reached more than $11bn in settlements to resolve claims that firefighting foam and other products containing their Pfas-polluted drinking water. None admitted wrongdoing.

events.title: Investors see surge in US Treasury yields emerging as new market risk
events.summary: The recent rise in US bond yields is emerging as a new source of investor anxiety after the 10-Year Treasury rose to a level not seen in almost two decades. A Bank of America fund manager survey on Tuesday said 33 per cent of respondents saw a “disorderly rise in bond yields” as the biggest market risk, replacing artificial intelligence. The survey was released a day after the yield on the 10-year Treasury passed 5 per cent. The 10-year yield rose to as high as 5.041 per cent earlier in the day – its highest since July 2007 – pushing up borrowing costs for consumers and companies. The rise in bond yields dragged down Wall Street's main indexes, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average suffering a loss of 328 points, or 0.63 per cent. Analysts have attributed the recent increase in bond yields to rising oil prices and inflation fears stemming from the Iran war, concerns about the US fiscal direction and spending by AI companies. Investors are now increasingly looking to the Federal Reserve to clamp down on inflation. Traders have all but locked in that the US Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points on Wednesday, with the UAE Central Bank likely to follow because of the dirham’s peg to the dollar. The rise in US Treasury yields come as some energy exporters in the Gulf lose out on revenue from the Iran war, which could make it more expensive to borrow. For countries with lower revenue and higher spending needs, government reserve funds and possibly sovereign wealth funds could be called on to assist with projects, said Rachel Ziemba, founder of geopolitical risk firm Ziemba Insights. “And so those issues, more so than where US rates are, are arguably more important,” she said. Ms Ziemba also said the region has been investing more in US equities and private equity, rather than in Treasury bonds and similar dynamics. “And I think that trend is likely to continue,” she said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the recent rise in bond yields on “global issues”, with the rise in US Treasury yields occurring alongside others across advanced economies as part of a broader global bond rout. Mr Bessent acknowledged the recent increase also reflected the “need to address the [US] deficit”, which recently passed $40 trillion. Mr Bessent told politicians during his testimony on Capitol Hill that the buyback programme was a success, repeating his claim the US bond market has been the best-performing in the developed world since President Donald Trump began his second term. The Treasury Department last week announced it was seeking to buy back $6 billion of government debt, triple the size of its normal operations, in an effort to calm the market. The department previously announced it would double the size of the programme. “There is a counter-factual of what would it ​have done – and we then proceeded to have the two most successful Treasury auctions that we've ‌had in 20 years,” he said. Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, said he believes low interest rates over the past 10 years have warped perceptions about the current Treasury levels. “If you look across history, a 10-year 5 per cent Treasury is not unusual, he said. “I think people need to be recalibrated.”

events.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
events.summary: The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort. Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up." The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter. Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present." Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm. Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

events.title: '60 Minutes' ratings tanked in the season debut under Bari Weiss
events.summary: CBS News' storied "60 Minutes" telecast saw a major ratings decline under top editor Bari Weiss. Bloomberg/Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The new-look "60 Minutes" suffered a major decline in viewership in its season debut. New lead producer Nick Bilton and top editor Bari Weiss spent the summer updating the telecast. About 7.9 million people watched the episode, down from about 10 million last year. CBS News' "60 Minutes" is off to a rocky start on the viewership front under its new leadership. Ratings for the "60 Minutes" season premiere on Sunday night plunged more than 20% from last year, according to data from Nielsen. About 7.9 million people watched the episode, orchestrated by new lead producer Nick Bilton, who was selected by top CBS News editor Bari Weiss in May. Last fall, just over 10 million people tuned in to the launch of "60 Minutes." Key context: The NFL game lead-in to "60 Minutes" was much weaker than last year, when Lamar Jackson's Baltimore Ravens faced Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. The premiere was "a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS," according to a memo that Bilton, Weiss, and network president Tom Cibrowski sent to CBS News staffers on Sunday. CBS News touted the online viewership of "60 Minutes," saying the news program roughly tripled its social media reach. Highlights of the episode included an interview with the US Air Force pilot who survived after being shot down in Iran and a profile on Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay as the NFL season kicked off. The episode also had interviews with so-called "pardon brokers" who sell wealthy clients on their supposed ability to influence presidential pardons. Bilton and Weiss spent the summer revamping "60 Minutes" after a choppy stretch in which correspondents Scott Pelley , Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, and Anderson Cooper left the storied news program. Pelley was fired by Bilton after publicly questioning his new boss' qualifications , pressing him on why Vega and Alfonsi were let go, and accusing Weiss of "murdering" the "60 Minutes" telecast. Longtime correspondents Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, and Jon Wertheim decided to stay at "60 Minutes" after Bilton pledged to uphold high journalistic standards, telling their colleagues that they "don't want to see 60 Minutes die." Bilton has put his touch on "60 Minutes" by modernizing its graphics and bringing on contributors like correspondent Ross Douthat, who came over from The New York Times in July. Weiss has ruffled some feathers since David Ellison, the CEO of CBS parent Paramount Skydance, put her in charge of CBS News last fall. The former New York Times opinion editor, who's known for her anti-woke views, has  faced accusations of political bias  and editorial interference that she has denied.
