events.title: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI
events.summary: 2026 midterm elections: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI Sep 15, 2026 | By Ginny Badanes, General Manager, Tech for Society, Microsoft As Americans prepare to vote this November, artificial intelligence is changing how many people find and understand election information. Some voters are deliberately turning to AI tools with questions about candidates, ballot measures, election procedures, and issues that matter to their communities. Others are encountering AI-generated summaries at the top of search results. In either case, AI is increasingly becoming a front door to election information. This shift is happening quickly. More than 30% of the U.S. working-age population now uses AI (Microsoft AI Diffusion Index, Q1 2026; Microsoft, AI Adoption Across the United States ) . These tools can help people understand complicated topics, compare information, and explore unfamiliar issues. But election information can also present some challenges for AI. It is highly local, changes quickly, and can be incomplete, contested, or stripped of essential context. The answer is not to steer voters away from AI, it is to help people use it wisely, particularly when the information may influence aspects of their voting experience, such as how, when, and where they cast their ballot. That is why, on National Voter Registration Day , a day when our brands and products come together to encourage civic participation , we’re launching the next phase of our voter education initiative, Check. Recheck. Vote . This year, the campaign will equip voters with practical AI literacy skills for the 2026 election season. We launched Check. Recheck. Vote. in 2024 to help voters recognize the risks posed by deceptive AI-generated content. Deepfakes and other deceptive media remain a serious concern. But in conversations with voters and election organizations, we are also hearing about a broader and more immediate challenge. Millions of people now encounter election information through AI-generated answers, and many are not sure how to determine whether those answers are current, complete, or reliable. The updated campaign gives voters three straightforward steps: Check the sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer. Look for where the information came from, who published it, and when it was last updated. Be cautious when an answer provides no sources. Recheck important details by visiting the original sources and comparing what other credible sources say. This is especially important for fast-changing or location-specific information. Vote based on current information from your state or local election website, including official guidance on registration, voting options, deadlines, and polling locations. At the center of the campaign is a new 75-second video that shows how an AI-generated answer can appear during an ordinary election-related search, explains where these answers can fall short, and offers simple steps voters can take before relying on them. The campaign website pairs the video with practical guidance and links to authoritative election resources, including state-by-state voting information and tools for educators. We are working with the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and the National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) to scale the reach of this campaign across all fifty states and the territories and to point voters to accurate information directly from state and local election officials so they can participate with confidence. We believe that civics and voter education start well before a citizen is old enough to vote. That’s why we are also investing in efforts to extend AI voter literacy education in the classroom. The campaign website includes a classroom activity to help students examine how AI may shape the election information they encounter, practice verifying claims, and keep their own judgment at the center of the process. We are also amplifying our impact on this important issue by supporting the News Literacy Project . We’re also proud to announce today that, in partnership with iCivics, we are launching Village Square – a new Minecraft Education civic learning experience that helps students explore how communities make decisions and solve shared challenges. The game brings concepts such as dialogue, participation, and collective decision-making to life through immersive gameplay. Village Square gives educators and families an engaging, nonpartisan way to help young people practice listening to different perspectives, weighing trade-offs and working together to build stronger communities. Finally, we know that credible local reporting remains essential to informed civic participation, and that reporting is under strain in many communities. In Washington state, Microsoft is partnering with the Associated Press Fund for Journalism to expand election coverage for 10 local newsrooms operating 14 news websites. Participating newsrooms receive access to AP election results and race calls, vote tabulations, state-specific maps and graphics, and resources that help local journalists connect national and statewide developments to the communities they serve. The newsrooms represent communities from Seattle to Spokane and the Wenatchee Valley. Their work complements the reporting of the Associated Press, helping trusted, fact-based election coverage and results reach communities that might otherwise lack access. This investment reflects a broader reality. Voters need more than information. They need reliable sources that can provide context, ask hard questions, correct mistakes, and explain what national developments mean at the local level. Microsoft’s Support for the 2026 Midterms Voters aren’t the only ones navigating this AI moment, so are the people running campaigns and conducting elections, all while facing an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. Microsoft has long supported the security and resilience of campaigns and elections. In 2018, we launched AccountGuard to help political campaigns and democracy-focused organizations defend against cyberattacks, and during the 2024 election cycle we joined dozens of other technology companies in the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections . Here’s how that commitment continues today: Equipping election officials. With The Elections Group, International IDEA, Ready for Tuesday and Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Lab, we launched the free, open-source AI + Elections Skills Hub : prompts, sample AI agents, and draft policies for responsible adoption. It’s already reached 1,000+ officials across 45 states. Strengthening cybersecurity. We’ve deployed Microsoft Sentinel to several state and local election offices for stronger threat detection, and we’re also supporting select election and political stakeholders with MDASH to find and fix software vulnerabilities faster. Countering bomb hoaxes.

( LinkedIn: Direct Selling Australia ) Under-fire multi-level-marketing company MONAT, accused of misleading selling practices, has used an industry showcase at Parliament House to promote its legitimacy. The inaugural showcase, hosted by industry body Direct Selling Australia, was held weeks after an ABC investigation into MONAT. Critics say Parliament House should not be used for commercial ventures and are calling for better oversight on who is allowed to host events in the halls of power. Representatives of a multi-level-marketing company accused of making misleading and exaggerated income and lifestyle claims have used an industry showcase at Parliament House in Canberra to tout its legitimacy and tell followers it has been "discussed in parliament". The Florida-born hair and skincare company MONAT has come under fire with allegations that its representatives are making embellished sales pitches to recruit women into the multi-level-marketing scheme — including flaunting new cars, trips to tropical locations, and the ability to work from anywhere — while 93 per cent of its sellers make little to no money. An Instagram story shows MONAT vice-president Jen Usher representing the company at the event. ( Instagram: jen_usher ) It has been investigated twice in the United States over misleading product and income claims, and the ACCC has been urged to investigate its Australian sellers over whether their practices breach consumer law . MONAT's social media claims have renewed serious concerns about hiring out Parliament House rooms for commercial purposes, and businesses using them to suggest parliamentary endorsement. A MONAT influencer writes about the importance of the showcase being held at Parliament House. ( Instagram: bek.sharma ) Hosted by Direct Selling Australia (DSA), the inaugural showcase came just two weeks after the ABC investigation. DSA is the national body representing network marketing companies like MONAT, which is a paying member. MONAT's vice-president and managing director of Australia and New Zealand, Jen Usher, sat on the board in 2024-2025. Ms Usher attended the event, alongside one of the company's top sellers, and both spruiked the event on their social media accounts. Six politicians were tagged in a DSA LinkedIn post as joining the event, including federal Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres. Mr Ayres declined to answer questions from the ABC. A post from one of the MONAT sellers saying MONAT was "discussed in parliament". ( Instagram: melissamunro._x ) Several MONAT representatives posted to their social media accounts to promote the showcase as a "powerful reminder that social selling is a legitimate, regulated industry". "Seeing our work discussed in parliament is a huge achievement," one representative wrote. "To see our industry being represented and having conversations inside Parliament House is pretty bloody cool," another wrote. Former NSW Supreme Court judge and chair of the Centre for Public Integrity, Anthony Whealy, said claiming legitimacy through presence in Parliament House was misleading. He said it was "not a good look" and asked whether Parliament House should be used for commercial purposes. Former NSW Supreme Court Judge Anthony Whealy questions whether Parliament House should be used for commercial ventures. ( ABC News ) Independent senator David Pocock said events at Parliament House should be used as a "force for good". "I do not believe parliamentary events should be used for fundraising or for the commercial benefit or endorsement of individual companies," he said. "Historically, there has been fairly poor oversight of the kind of events conducted inside Parliament House, and it is something I have pursued at Senate estimates and raised with the presiding officers. "I would be very uncomfortable having my photo used for promotional or endorsement purposes that I was not aware of or did not agree to." David Pocock says there needs to be better oversight of events conducted in Parliament House. ( ABC News: Adam Kennedy ) ABC's Four Corners recently highlighted these concerns, and whether stronger safeguards were needed around commercial interests and lobbying inside Parliament House. A statement from MONAT Global sent to the ABC by one of its Australian representatives said the company was "proud" to have been part of the event.

events.title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique security and economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
events.summary: Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”. Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States. Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation. “The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies. “Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.” While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country. That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks. Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels. European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy. Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence. “Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union , with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.” The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe. But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force. French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.

In his first speech, the senator advocated support for local manufacturing, but said the clothes were made overseas because it was too expensive to do so in Australia. Senator Babet has flagged his intention to retire when his term expires in 2028. "Christian nationalist" Senator Ralph Babet's new fashion line, which includes Australian flag towels, mugs and socks, is made in South America and Asia. The lone United Australia Party senator launched "Staunch by Senator Babet" this month, a line that carries shirts with political and religious slogans. Among them are shirts depicting the senator smoking a cigar, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with the caption "zero testosterone detected", a shirt featuring "the world is controlled by Satanic paedophiles", as well as shirts with biblical references. The ABC contacted the support line for Senator Babet's clothing brand and was told that the products were mostly made in South America and Asia, and then sent to the United States or another country for screen printing. Senator Babet confirmed the products were manufactured offshore, with screen printing done in Australia. After the ABC spoke directly with Senator Babet, a new T-shirt design appeared on his website calling to "defund the ABC", which notes that other parties and senators also sell merchandise. Staunch by Senator Babet added this design after the ABC spoke with the senator about his clothing line. ( Staunch by Senator Babet ) Senator Babet entered parliament on a platform of putting Australia "first", and in his first speech to parliament called on Australians and the parliament to support local manufacturing. "We must become a nation which makes things again. Our manufacturing sector has been decimated and sent offshore, once again at the behest of unelected global bureaucrats. Let's take the brakes off our businesses and entrepreneurs. Let them work. Let them produce. Let them create wealth," Senator Babet said in 2022. "We need to ensure that we give Australian businesses strong support and an unencumbered legislative pathway so they can grow, compete and become major players on the world stage." Senator Babet told the ABC he was not using an Australian manufacturer because it was cheaper to make clothing overseas, and high taxes and energy costs made it prohibitive to manufacture onshore. "If you can find a T-shirt manufacturer in Australia, I would use them, but there isn't one," Senator Babet said. "These days everything is made in China." Staunch by Senator Babet sells products carrying the Australian flag, including this towel, though the products are not manufactured in Australia. ( Staunch by Senator Babet ) Senator Babet has recently used clips of his speeches to the Senate to promote his brand on social media, with for-sale shirts and links to his website overlaid on videos where he advocates for more limited government. But he told the ABC the fashion line was a personal project and self-funded, with no parliamentary resources used on the brand. His fashion project would not support the United Australia Party but instead would go towards advertising for causes he supported, such as lowering migration. The senator said it had not yet been declared because 'Staunch' was not yet making enough money to warrant formal disclosure. Labor attacks attendance record of 'Ghost of the Senate' In February, Senator Babet announced he would not re-contest his position when his term expired in 2028, saying he had "failed" as a senator to protect free speech. Senator Babet was the only successful candidate who ran under Clive Palmer's United Australia Party banner at the 2022 election, despite the mining billionaire spending $117 million on that campaign through his company Mineralogy. Ralph Babet was elected as a senator for Victoria in 2022 under Clive Palmer's United Australia Party banner. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) On Monday, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher taunted the senator over his attendance in the Senate, after his question was handed to One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts to be asked. "I think that's the second week in a row you've had Senator Babet's question. You lucky guy! I wonder where the ghost of the Senate is," Senator Gallagher said. "We never see him anymore, do we? I noticed he did launch a clothing range a few days ago though, so he had time to do that.

events.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
events.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known. By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development. Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether. His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%. The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress. Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact. "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

events.title: My daughter is obsessed with Snoopy. I woke up at 3:30 a.m. to hunt down Starbucks' new viral cup.
events.summary: Charlotte Mandrier bought the Snoopy cup for her daughter Courtesy of Charlotte Mandrier Charlotte Mandrier's 9-year-old daughter has a deep love of Peanuts and Snoopy. Mandrier's daughter watches "The Great Pumpkin" year-round and listens to its soundtrack. With her birthday days away, Mandrier secretly hunted down the new Starbucks collection. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Charlotte Mandrier. It has been edited for length and clarity. On Monday, September 14, I was cleaning up my inbox and deleting emails when I saw that Starbucks was collaborating with the Peanuts brand to sell merchandise inspired by " The Great Pumpkin ." I remembered last year when Starbucks released a small number of bear cups . My daughter, who is 9, had wanted one but hadn't managed to get hold of one. She was so disappointed. She clearly hadn't known about the Snoopy cups that were going on sale, or I would have heard about it from her. She is obsessed with Peanuts, Snoopy, and "The Great Pumpkin." She watches the movie all year long As an autistic person , she has a special interest in Peanuts, specifically "The Great Pumpkin." She watches it all year long, even though it is a very fall movie. She listens to the music from the film's soundtrack. She was born in Santa Rosa, where the museum commemorating Charles Schulz — the cartoonist who created the Peanuts comic — is located. When she was little, she went to a camp at the museum and learned to ice skate at Snoopy's Home Ice next door. She even looks like Linus. She loves everything about this brand. Charlotte Mandrier's daughter loves everything related to Peanuts. Courtesy of Charlotte Mandrier As it happened, her birthday is in two days. So when I saw that these limited-edition Snoopy cups and other merchandise celebrating the movie would be on sale, I told my husband I was going to try to get one for her. I woke up in the middle of the night I set my alarm for Tuesday morning at 3:30 a.m., quietly sneaking out of the house to arrive at our closest Starbucks in downtown Chevy Chase at 4 a.m., when it opens. Charlotte Mandrier wants to surprise her daughter with her Snoopy Starbucks cup. Courtesy of Charlotte Mandrier Walking six blocks to get there, I only saw one other woman on the street. It turned out she was going to the same Starbucks to wait in line, too. When I got there, no one was in line yet, and I felt so relieved. I had imagined that there would already be a huge line, with people hoping to take all the stock to resell it later. I suppose that since it was a fairly commercial area, rather than a residential area, people didn't think to go there to get the merchandise. Slowly, others arrived. There were three of us waiting for the merchandise, and three regulars who were just there to get their coffee. Charlotte Mandrier only saw about 10 Snoopy cups at her local Starbucks. Courtesy of Charlotte Mandrier Although they were meant to open the doors at 4 a.m., apparently, there was a staffing issue, and they didn't open until 5 a.m. The regulars said that it wasn't normal for the shop to open late. The lights were on, but we couldn't see anyone inside. We tried knocking because we weren't sure if someone was there, and just didn't know we were waiting. We were desperate to get the good stuff. There were about 10 Snoopy cups While we waited, I used my phone to take photos of the merchandise and count how many cups were available. I could see about 10. Then someone finally unlocked and opened the doors for us. Once I got in, I bought a Snoopy cup, a tote bag, a keychain, a mug, and some pins. It came to about $200. Charlotte Mandrier spent $200 in Starbucks merchandise for her daughter. Courtesy of Charlotte Mandrier One of the regulars who was there got swept up in the hype and got a cup, even though it wasn't why she'd come. It was incredibly exciting that I had managed to get the stuff. I was so excited, imagining my daughter's face in two days when she opens her birthday presents. Sneaking back into the house at 5:30 a.m. and hiding it all away, I pretended I had just woken up. As soon as she sees on YouTube that these cups were for sale, I know she'll be disappointed, thinking that, like last year, she missed out. I'll give an Oscar-winning performance, telling her I wish we could have gotten there sooner, and maybe we can look for Snoopy cups that people are selling online. And then, in two days, I'll give her all the Peanuts presents. I really cannot wait. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely on Monday. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Relay — a startup outpaced by bigger platforms — is one version of the story playing out right now. But plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

events.title: Suncorp's debt collector engaging in 'worst kind' of bullying, former ACCC chair says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Diane and Scott Walker spent months fighting an insurance claim they likened to "bullying". ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Debt collector ARMA Group spent months harassing and intimidating 81-year-old Diane Walker into paying an insurance claim she was not responsible for. ARMA, acting on behalf of insurance giant Suncorp, ended the ordeal with an apology to Ms Walker and financial compensation for the distress caused, but only after months of legal threats and pressure to pay. "They were rather bullying-type letters … it's in the back of your mind all the time," Ms Walker said. ARMA's website says its workflows are "AI-driven", boasting it takes the company "less than two minutes to set up a smart payment plan and no manual intervention is required". Ms Walker's case is just the tip of the iceberg as the consumer watchdog takes ARMA Group and Force Legal, both owned by Credit Clear Limited, to court, alleging that between them they sent 320,000 debt enforcement notices to individuals that were allegedly misleading. Former ACCC chair Allan Fels says he is "very concerned" about the conduct of debt collector ARMA Group. ( ABC News: Patrick Rocca ) Legal experts are appalled and say it is a clear breach of Australian consumer laws. "This is Robodebt 2.0 of the worst form," said Allan Fels, former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). "I'm very concerned … this seems to be the worst kind of illegal, deceptive conduct applied to bully, intimidate, frighten. "It's traumatic for the individual to be confronted in a Robodebt situation with no opportunity to respond or fight back, or talk to someone, or explain their personal circumstances. "There needs to be a serious, substantial crackdown on this kind of approach." If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@proton.me Just before Christmas, Ms Walker was involved in a minor two-vehicle car crash she was not responsible for, and that caused no damage. Diane Walker was sent multiple legal threats for a car insurance claim she was never liable for. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The other driver's insurer, AAMI, a subsidiary of Suncorp, contacted Ms Walker looking to recover costs, despite having no evidence. "I would have emailed them at least half a dozen times saying, 'Send me some photos, send me something that demonstrates that at least something happened,'" said Scott Walker, who stepped in as his mother's representative on the claim. About two months after AAMI first contacted Ms Walker, it engaged its debt collector, ARMA Group, to recover the funds. Without providing evidence, the debt collector concluded that Ms Walker was "liable". Previously a freelance camera operator for the ABC, Mr Walker said he spent hundreds of hours trying to make sense of ARMA's communication. "It was just this level of intimidation … the wording sounded very much like there's been some legal decision made, some type of independent, judicial system that has found an outcome," he said. Ms Walker and her son said ARMA's letters were relentless. Despite initially telling Ms Walker she had been found "liable" for the car accident, ARMA began threatening court action, suggesting culpability remained unresolved. One letter said: "If you choose to dispute the issue with arguments that are not relevant — such as claiming there is no dashcam footage or no photos of the vehicles at the moment of impact — we will have no choice but to escalate the matter further. "You are welcome to present those arguments in court if you believe they support your case. If you are found liable, you would be liable for court fees as well." ARMA Group was initially claiming $1,175.51 from Ms Walker. But after three months, the company increased the amount to $1,395.51 without explanation. Mr Walker was then sent a separate claim, arguing he was now responsible for the accident, even though he wasn't there at the time. Scott Walker says he spent hundreds of hours on the insurance claim before receiving an apology. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "The system's not designed to have a sensible conversation with someone at the other end; it's a system that is designed to make you pay," Mr Walker said. ARMA Group did not respond to questions from ABC News. Suncorp did not provide an on the record response to the ABC's questions. events.title: John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bank
events.summary: Exclusive: Britain is understood to have been formally invited to become founding member of multilateral lender John Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks after Rachel Reeves rejected the move. The chancellor is understood to be actively considering a bid to join the proposed Canada-led defence, security and resilience bank (DSRB), which proponents say could help the UK fund defence projects at lower cost, before planned talks with his Canadian counterpart this week. When he was defence secretary, Healey was understood to have been a strong advocate for keeping UK observers present at Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney’s, defence bank talks, despite resistance from the Treasury, which wanted to shut off those international discussions. Reeves, his predecessor as chancellor, was concerned the bank would not address the UK’s defence procurement issues and was more focused on lending to smaller defence firms in nations with lower credit ratings. The UK has had a AA credit rating since 2016. Healey, who has long been a proponent of multilateral funding mechanisms, met the Canadian finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, twice at a G20 summit in North Carolina two weeks ago. They are due to meet again in the UK this week, when the two men are – according to sources – likely to discuss the defence bank, and both are expected to be at EU finance minister talks in Dublin later this week. Canada is understood to have already formally invited the UK to become a founding member of the bank, along with eight other countries including Ukraine and Turkey. Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, accusing Keir Starmer and his chancellor, Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk because the defence spending package fell £13bn short of what he argued was required. As chancellor, he is expected to avoid setting a target date for reaching 3% defence spending in next month’s budget and instead is planning to set out a pathway to reaching the goal at the 2027 spending review. The DSRB could play a role in this by using financial leverage, separate from the balance sheets of ​already indebted nations, to boost defence investment. But it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments to become a major player. Reeves announced at the Nato summit in Ankara in July that the UK would join the Netherlands, Finland and Poland to launch a new lender called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism. She said the MDM would help the UK with procurement – saving the UK as much as 20% – and stockpiling, which would give taxpayers better value for money while allowing government to borrow at a low rate to fund defence. The UK has committed an initial £600m to the new lender. The former chancellor had called for the two rival international defence financing schemes to merge, arguing that it made sense for countries to only fund one institution that could work for all nations. In addition to overlaps with existing initiatives, there were also understood to be concerns in the Treasury over the amount of capital that countries would need to commit while public finances are strained. The UK’s initial capital contribution would be between £1bn and £2bn over three years. The DSRB has ​been seeking to raise around €100bn, which it would use to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers. A government spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity. “We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary.”

events.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
events.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters. Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports , is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof). Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion. Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval. More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%). Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%. events.title: US data centers could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt The AI race has grown so frenzied that, by 2035, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined. Over the next decade, data centers are expected to be the second-strongest driver of natural gas demand growth after LNG exports. The facilities could consume about 18 billion cubic feet per day, according to a new report from BloombergNEF , nearly double the amount the organization predicted just nine months ago. The new forecast takes into account that not all announced data center projects will be completed. Data centers that produce power onsite have grabbed headlines in recent months, with Meta , Microsoft , Google , and Amazon all announcing plans for new natural gas power plants that will bypass the grid. Projects such as these will consume 2.9 billion to 3.4 billion cubic feet per day by 2035. That’s about as much as all data centers consume today , including natural gas used to generate power for the grid. But onsite-powered data centers could represent just a fraction of overall demand growth, according to BloombergNEF. By the middle of the next decade, grid-connected data centers are predicted to drive an additional 15 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas consumption by the power sector. To put that in context, that’s five times more demand growth through 2035 than from all other grid-connected sectors combined. If that stunning demand growth materializes, it could nudge natural gas prices higher. Much of today’s data center buildout relies on stable natural gas prices, which have prevailed in recent years. But analysts at Noreva think that might be a false hope. The combined impact of the data center boom and rising LNG exports could cause prices to soar . Even if tech companies’ balance sheets can bear such a surge, utility ratepayers might not be able to. Burning one cubic foot of natural gas releases the equivalent of 60 grams of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, including extraction, processing, and distribution, according to the IEA. The additional demand from data centers will generate 1 million metric tons more greenhouse gas pollution daily. That’s about 12% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions today. events.title: How the Copilot Creators Collective is shaping the future of creativity and AI literacy
events.summary: The New Media Movement: How the Copilot Creators Collective is Shaping the Future of Creativity and AI Literacy A year ago, Microsoft brought together a group of Filipino creators around a shared question: what becomes possible when creativity, community, and AI come together? That question became the starting point for the Copilot Creators Collective, a community built around a clear mission: to help more Filipinos understand, explore, and use AI responsibly through the voices of creators they trust. One year later, that mission has been brought to life by CCC members who are not only experimenting with Microsoft Copilot in their own work, but also translating AI into stories, conversations, and learning moments that feel practical, familiar, and human. At the heart of the Collective is Microsoft’s vision of empowering every person and organization on the planet to achieve more. For the CCC, that vision extends from creators to the communities they reach. Through campaigns, learning sessions, and creator-led storytelling, members have helped broaden AI literacy and advocate for responsible AI use by showing how Copilot can support real moments in work, life, education, creativity, and learning. “Over the past year, the Copilot Creators Collective has shown us what happens when Filipino creators are given the space, tools, and community to explore AI with purpose,” said Josh Aquino, Head of Communication of Microsoft Philippines. “But the Collective was never built for creators alone. It was built so more Filipinos could see AI in the context of everyday life—through people they trust, stories they relate to, and examples that show how Copilot can help them create, learn, work, and solve problems responsibly.” One Year of Learning, Experimenting, and Creating Together In its first year, the CCC’s mission moved from idea to action through the creators who carried it into different communities. Across learning spaces, workplace conversations, and education campaigns, members helped make AI feel less abstract and more useful to the people it was meant to serve. At the YSEALI Bootcamp for Digital Creators, Isa Rodriguez, CJ Salvador, and Jax Reyes brought creator-led perspectives to a regional initiative designed to equip young Southeast Asian leaders with digital storytelling and responsible technology skills. Organized in partnership with the U.S. Department of State through the Young Southeast Asian Leaders Initiative, the bootcamp gathered 81 Attendees from across the region, representing multiple nations and communities. The initiative provided a platform for CCC members to show how Microsoft 365 and Copilot can support productivity, content creation, and responsible experimentation. Their participation showed how AI literacy can start with people who understand the realities of digital storytelling and can speak to peers in a way that feels grounded, practical, and approachable. That same role came through in Microsoft’s Work Trend Index campaign, which emphasized that while AI is already embedded in everyday work, the next frontier is helping people and organizations turn individual experimentation into trusted, repeatable, and scalable ways of working. Through this campaign, Trixie Esguerra-Bugia helped make insights on AI adoption, productivity, and the future of work more relatable for everyday professionals and creators. Her own use of Copilot reflects the practical value she helps audiences see: it supports the behind-the-scenes work that makes content creation possible, from organizing shot lists to checking grammar and refining outlines. For creators working as one-human teams, she shows how AI can serve as a digital assistant that brings more structure and confidence to everyday work. In education, Alvin Santos and Reb Atadero helped bring the same message to Filipino teachers and learners through Microsoft’s campaign in partnership with the Department of Education. Leveraging DepEd’s nationwide network, the campaign showed how free tools such as Copilot Chat and Reading Progress can address classroom needs at scale. In just 21 weeks, it reached 3,431 students across eight regions, analyzed 8,381 reading submissions, trained 2,002 teachers, and achieved 91.5 percent teacher satisfaction. By connecting AI to everyday teaching, literacy, and student support, Alvin and Reb helped frame it as a practical aid for educators and learners alike. Alvin’s own experience reinforces this point: he has used Copilot as a creative sounding board and to develop lesson plans tailored to French non-native English speakers. The Collective’s work also shows how AI can support more ambitious ideas behind the scenes. Ceej Tantengco-Malolos experienced this while organizing an art exhibit for women’s sports. With Copilot and a small team, she created display mockups, drafted media invitations, and built a promotional plan for an event that might have otherwise felt difficult to take on. Her example adds another layer to the CCC’s first-year story: responsible AI is not only about learning the tool, but using it to bring meaningful ideas to life. Other members of the Collective echo this sense of possibility. Buji Babiera shared how Copilot helped him gather themes from different parts of the world for a local story under a tight deadline. Abi Maravilla described Copilot as a sounding board that helps simplify the complex and organize ideas without becoming overwhelmed. Andi Lopez shared how it helps turn scattered thoughts into something clearer and more meaningful, while also supporting work such as marketing pitch decks and data analysis for esports commentary. Seen together, these efforts move the CCC’s story forward from experimentation to impact. In its first year, the Collective helped broaden AI literacy by meeting Filipinos where they are: creators learning to work more efficiently, professionals navigating the future of work, educators looking for practical classroom support, and communities discovering how AI can help them start, organize, teach, create, and solve problems more responsibly. One year in, the Copilot Creators Collective stands as both a milestone and a starting point. Its first year shows how Filipino creators are already using AI to work more efficiently, think more expansively, and tell stories with greater confidence. It also shows that the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by people: creators who ask better questions, share what they learn, and use new tools to bring more thoughtful ideas into the world. “My first year with the Copilot Creator Collective was marked with remarkable firsts. It was my first time working with Microsoft Copilot and AI in general” said Alvin Santos. “And also, my first to be part of a project that fostered long-lasting partnerships with the brand and a thoughtfully curated bunch of amazing content creators. I’m raring to see what’s in store for the 2nd year!

events.title: SpaceX will try to put Starship in orbit for the first time on September 22
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt SpaceX is ready to perform the 14th test flight of its Starship mega-rocket, and now the company will finally try to put the upper stage into Earth’s orbit for the first time, the company announced Tuesday. The test launch is scheduled for September 22, with a 75-minute launch window opening at 7:15 a.m. CT. During the test launch, SpaceX plans to deploy the first batch of third-generation Starlinks into its network of 10,000 internet satellites. The company expects to launch 26 V3 satellites into orbit in this test flight. If successful, this will be the first Starship launch to generate revenue for SpaceX’s launch division (even if that revenue is coming from another division of the company). This will be the second Starship test launch since SpaceX became a publicly traded company in the largest IPO in history in June. The first came in July, when SpaceX successfully deployed V3 Starlink satellites for the first time — though those were only meant to test Starship’s deployment capability and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere after roughly 20 minutes. Getting Starship’s upper stage into orbit around Earth would represent a major milestone for SpaceX. The company has spent billions of dollars on the program and is now looking to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in favor of Starship. Founder and CEO Elon Musk has said that will happen once Starship is flying “reliably several times per week” to save “scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources.” SpaceX needs Starship to reliably reach orbit, return to Earth, and get quickly reused to fulfill the massive launch cadence promises that it made during the IPO process. Starship’s 14th test flight will only test the first part of that equation, though. Musk recently walked back previous claims that SpaceX might try to use its launch tower to catch the Starship upper stage during this flight, saying an explosion would be too big a setback for the company at this point. SpaceX also won’t try to catch the Super Heavy booster this time. The company has struggled with the booster during its last few test flights and has made multiple changes to try to prevent failures. Yet the booster still struggled to properly relight its engines after separating from the Starship upper stage on Flight 13 in July. For this mission, SpaceX said Tuesday that it made another round of “several modifications” to the booster’s hardware and software to “address issues seen on the previous flight.” SpaceX had far more success with the upper stage of Starship on Flight 13. While it did not reach orbit, it had a smooth flight through a simulated landing in the Indian Ocean. The upper stage didn’t even explode when it tipped over into the water, allowing SpaceX to spend the last few months capturing and slowly towing it back to its Texas headquarters. SpaceX said Tuesday that it has made additional changes to the Starship heat shield based on what it learned from studying the recovered upper stage from Flight 13. Jeanne Calment was the oldest verified person to have ever lived, passing away at 122. Despite Calment's extraordinary longevity, her home country, France, ranks 19th in the world for average life expectancy. The World Bank Group collected data on life expectancy at birth by country through 2024. Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live if mortality patterns remain the same throughout their life. The countries ranked highest tend to be wealthier, with robust healthcare systems and lower rates of early-life mortality . Meanwhile, the countries with the lowest life expectancy are all located in Africa, which often faces disease, malnutrition, and conflict. High mortality among infants and children and healthcare shortages on the continent significantly lower the life expectancy at birth. The US ranked 47th in the dataset, with an average life expectancy of 78.9 years. The World Bank Group used statistics from sources such as the United Nations and national statistical office databases. Business Insider did not include autonomous regions and territories listed in the data. events.title: As the politicians play catchup the tech bros agree: we may only have a decade left | John Crace
events.summary: AI on course to kill us all within 10 years? Donald Trump says: ‘Hold my Coke’ US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel W e can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account, Donald Trump has declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart. All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind. You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best. Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass the Turing test . Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference. Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us. It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die. You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking. Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis. And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds , had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid. “There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years. People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one. And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion. And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated. So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak. There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters CenterPoint Energy confirms intruder helped themselves to customer information 16 hours ago September's Windows 11 patch needs an emergency patch of its own 16 hours ago Microsoft account refuseniks have another way of installing Windows 18 hours ago Microsoft drafts feel-good AI model guidelines and wants your input 1 day ago HBO Max Reddit account compromised to serve ClickFix attacks 1 day ago Iranian state cyber actors are targeting individuals using social messaging apps to deploy surveillance and data-stealing malware on their Windows machines, three Western governments warned. In all observed cases, Chosen Brick has infected Windows systems exclusively. Iran has used it since at least 2025 to take over individuals’ devices, stealing their contacts, emails, and social media messages, which allows the spies to track people’s movements, the FBI, UK National Cyber Security Centre, and the Netherlands’ General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) said on Tuesday. “Iran almost certainly uses cyber activity to support the repression of individuals who are seen as a threat to the regime, such as dissidents, activists and journalists,” the security advisory said. “In some cases, the Iranian intelligence services have plotted to kidnap or conduct lethal operations against individuals internationally, who they perceive as enemies of the regime.” These attacks typically begin with WhatsApp and Telegram messages, purportedly coming from individuals and organizations that the victim knows and trusts. The Iranian spies do a significant amount of research to prepare for these social engineering campaigns . By the time they send the initial message via a social media app, they have “extensive” knowledge of the targeted individual, their contacts, and relevant industry organizations to make the phony messages more believable, according to the agencies. After building rapport with the mark, the attackers convince them to download and open a file that appears to be a legitimate application. Specifically: Pictory, RunwayML, Norton Antivirus, Telegram, Adobe Flash Player, and KeePass are among the legitimate applications the malicious files have been made to resemble, the government agencies said. Upon opening the file, the malware executes without the victim’s knowledge, and will survive a reboot of the target device. Chosen Brick also adds exclusions to Microsoft Defender antivirus in an attempt to evade detection, and then connects to Telegram for command-and-control (C2) communications using a victim-specific Telegram bot. While the malware hasn’t yet been observed to automate lateral movement across the network, this is “technically possible,” the advisory noted. It does, however, download additional malware and set up persistence for new payloads on infected devices, using the same registry key that Chosen Brick uses to establish its own persistence on a Windows device: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Other features include enumerating running processes and system information, capturing screen and audio content, stealing emails, along with Telegram and WhatsApp data from web browsers, and wiping the computer system. “Organizations that are concerned Chosen Brick has been executed should contact their IT providers, either internal or external, to investigate,” the US, UK, and the Netherlands warned. “As this actor targets personal devices, not just corporate devices, organizations are recommended to circulate this with their staff that are likely to be targeted and support them in checking their personal devices too.” The Western agencies’ latest Iran alert follows a series of water and energy cyberattacks that researchers and media reports have linked to Iran, although the US and UK governments have stopped short of formally attributing them, as the military conflict between Iran and the US approaches its seventh month.

events.title: New AI tool lets influencers ‘scale themselves like software’
events.summary: The News The tech-focused creator Emily Higgins is speaking directly into the camera about the importance of a good hook for a social media video — she does what looks like three takes, each with a slightly different script. But Higgins only filmed one video. The other two were AI-edited, using a new tool from New York-based tech-media startup Avail that allows brands to create dozens of variants of video ads recorded by human influencers. The creatorAPI platform, which launched Tuesday, points to a social-media future in which content created or augmented with AI is increasingly common. It’s also a response to the rise of so-called “synthetic influencers,” completely fake avatars that can hawk goods on the internet. Instead, the tool will allow creators to “scale themselves like software,” said Avail CEO Chris Giliberti. It’s designed so the human creator authorizes all of their different videos: Brands can fix recording mistakes, test out different intros, or create variations that target different geographies or audiences. Using a technique known as “dark posting,” all the different ads won’t show up on the creator’s profile, but will proliferate into users’ feeds. Avail put together a cocktail of third-party AI models to create the tool. Know More Giliberti acknowledged the tool could be controversial, given how difficult it is for an untrained eye to tell the differences between AI-edited videos and the growing public pushback to anything tinged with AI, especially in the creative space. “There’s this purity that people expect from creatives, like they’re always the last people that are allowed to adopt productivity tools,” he said. “I just think it’s really unfortunate that software engineers are able to crank out 10 times more code with [AI] tools and that’s palatable... but the second a creator adopts a tool like this, they’re shamed for it.” Notable As the technology improves, using AI to edit video for translation purposes is increasingly common: Amazon last week rolled out alternate-language versions of a popular German soap opera that were made using AI lip-dubbing.

events.title: The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control W hen Labour made the Bank of England independent in 1997, the idea was that the Bank set interest rates while the Treasury taxed and spent. Monetary policy was in Threadneedle Street, fiscal policy in Whitehall. But in August the Bank of England quietly slipped out that its key policy could cost the Treasury £120bn . That policy – quantitative tightening (QT) – clearly ought to be rethought and the policy of the Treasury indemnifying the Bank for its losses ended . Last year, ministers paid the Bank £17bn to cover these arguably notional losses – an amount considerably larger than the budget of the Ministry of Justice, which is dealing with a real prisons crisis. Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects. The financial crisis, Covid, war and fractious trade disputes have contributed to ending that world. The Bank bought up government bonds to support the economy via its quantitative easing (QE) programme. But the constitutional settlement – of an independent central bank working out on its own what to do with those bonds – has not caught up. The game is surely up when a former Bank deputy governor, Charlie Bean , acknowledges that independence cannot justify effectively giving power to an unelected monetary policy committee (MPC) over decisions with great consequences for public spending. The Treasury stands behind the losses – and gains – made by the bonds bought during QE and held in a Bank of England subsidiary, called the Asset Purchase Facility . The losses are being produced in three ways. First, the Bank is selling these gilts at current market prices. Because their yields are higher than when QE was operating, the gilts are worth less than the APF paid for them. Second, the APF generates a loss because the £500bn bonds on its balance sheet generate less income than the repayments, charged at the base rate, on the “loan” it took to buy them. Third, gilts bought above their value are booked as a loss when they mature. Labour created the indemnity after the 2009 crash. But it was George Osborne who turned it into a quarterly cash machine in 2012. When rates were low, the Treasury profited to the tune of £124bn. Once rates rose, the same mechanism went into reverse – and because it is an uncapped indemnity, even when the windfall has been repaid the Treasury carries on paying the Bank. Ministers should end this arrangement. No other major central bank carries on in this way. Whatever one thinks of the losses, making the Treasury settle them immediately turns monetary choices into fiscal interventions. A report this week says that the Bank and Treasury are drawing up changes to QT to reduce pressure on raising interest rates. Independence seems to have been discarded in favour of quiet coordination. The MPC’s decisions cannot be beyond challenge. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, calls the overall cost of QT “ neutral ” – but only, as the economist Patricia Pino points out, when assessed over six decades. In fact, billions in cash demands fall within a parliament. Governments do not set budgets, fight elections or run public services over 60 years. It is unsustainable for the Bank to make decisions and have ministers face voters for the political consequences. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks
events.summary: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development There have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop. Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them. ‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026 Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University. It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”. With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said. Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said. Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still. Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.” ‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026 This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system. One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios. “These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”. “If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work. Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test . The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet. Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”. 'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time.
